title: Patient Portals and Secure Messaging

sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe patient portals and secure messaging and how they differ from standard email and text messaging.
- Explain the benefits of patient portals and secure messaging for patients and for the medical office.
- Apply HIPAA Privacy and Security Rule safeguards to protect PHI during electronic communication.
- Recognize urgent and emergent concerns received through portal or messaging channels and escalate them promptly.
- Identify appropriate uses of email and text messaging for patient communication while safeguarding PHI.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

A patient portal is like a private online mailbox for your health information — only you (and people you allow) can open it with your own password.

### Question 2

Secure messaging is like passing notes inside a locked classroom instead of shouting across a crowded playground.

### Question 3

Just like a bank account needs a password before you can see your money, a portal needs a login before you can see your health information.

### Question 4

The EHR is the big filing cabinet the office uses, and the portal is the small window where a patient can peek at their own papers.

### Question 5

Portal messaging is like a sealed, signed envelope, while ordinary email is more like a postcard anyone can glance at.

### Question 6

A portal lets you look at your own test results, like checking your own report card — not anyone else's.

### Question 7

Portal messaging is for everyday questions — like asking a teacher about homework — not for emergencies, which need a 911 call right away.

### Question 8

If someone messages that they cannot breathe, that is like a fire alarm — you do not wait, you get them emergency help right away.

### Question 9

A portal is like a library open all night — you can use it whenever it fits your schedule.

### Question 10

If a helper needs to manage an account, you give them their own key — you never hand out your own password.

### Question 11

Signing up for a portal is like getting a key card for a building — you must prove who you are before you receive it.

### Question 12

You check a person's ID before handing over their package so it does not go to the wrong house.

### Question 13

The law says you get to see a copy of your own file — but not anyone else's.

### Question 14

Requesting a refill online is like ordering a book online instead of calling the store — faster and simpler.

### Question 15

Scheduling through a portal is like booking a restaurant table online instead of calling.

### Question 16

The portal is like getting your report card online right away instead of waiting for a letter.

### Question 17

Messaging is like leaving a note a friend can read when they are free, instead of playing phone tag.

### Question 18

A portal is like a health scrapbook you can flip through anytime to see where you have been and what happened.

### Question 19

For a small question, send a note through the safe portal — not a flare to the whole world.

### Question 20

When you can see your own game stats, you are more likely to care about improving them.

### Question 21

Only the owner of a locker — or someone they officially allow — can open it.

### Question 22

Getting an email is instant, while getting a letter takes days in the mail.

### Question 23

If you can check the answer yourself online, you do not need to call and ask.

### Question 24

A portal handles the easy paper-like tasks so people can focus on the harder jobs.

### Question 25

Online refill requests are like an express lane — quicker for everyone, but a pharmacist still checks the order.

### Question 26

A portal is like a self-checkout lane that handles the easy items quickly.

### Question 27

A reminder is like an alarm clock for an appointment — it helps you show up on time.

### Question 28

Secure messaging is like writing in a notebook instead of whispering — there is a record of what was said.

### Question 29

Sending a digital note saves the paper, ink, and stamp of mailing a letter.

### Question 30

When something is easy and works anytime, people are happier with the service.

### Question 31

Keeping a careful record is like saving receipts — it shows what happened and why.

### Question 32

A portal takes the easy chores off your plate so you can focus on the important ones.

### Question 33

PHI is your private health details with your name on them — like a diary that also has your address.

### Question 34

You have a right to your own report card, not to everyone else's.

### Question 35

Technical safeguards are like locks and alarms on a building that keep intruders out.

### Question 36

Encryption is like writing a secret code that only someone with the decoder ring can read.

### Question 37

You never share your locker combination, because then no one knows who opened it.

### Question 38

Always lock the door behind you so no one can walk into your account.

### Question 39

You open only the file you need for your job, not the whole filing cabinet.

### Question 40

A cashier's key opens the register, not the manager's safe — each role gets only the keys it needs.

### Question 41

Two-factor login is like needing both a key and a code to open a door — twice the protection.

### Question 42

A screen that locks itself is like a door that closes on its own when you forget.

### Question 43

An audit trail is like a sign-in sheet that shows who came and went and what they touched.

### Question 44

If a store loses your package, they are supposed to tell you — not keep it a secret.

### Question 45

The notice is like the rules sheet you get with a board game — it tells you how your information may be used.

### Question 46

You need a signed permission slip to share certain private details — a nod from a friend is not enough.

### Question 47

You would not talk about someone's private health details in a crowded cafeteria.

### Question 48

Work documents belong in the work safe, not in your personal backpack.

### Question 49

You would not hand new house keys to a stranger who simply asks — you check who they are first.

### Question 50

Turning your test paper so no one can copy it is a simple way to keep it private.

### Question 51

Administrative safeguards are the rules and training that teach everyone how to keep information safe.

### Question 52

If you see a strange person trying your neighbor's door, you tell someone — not keep it to yourself.

### Question 53

If a grade on your report card is wrong, you can ask the teacher to fix it — but the teacher reviews it first.

### Question 54

It is like asking for a list of who borrowed your book — a record of certain times your information was shared.

### Question 55

Send private health details through the locked, secure channel — not on a public bulletin board.

### Question 56

Do not write a secret on the outside of the envelope — keep it inside where only the recipient sees it.

### Question 57

Regular email is like a postcard that people along the way can read, while the portal is a sealed envelope.

### Question 58

A text can sit on a phone where others might see it, like a note left on a park bench.

### Question 59

The portal checks your ID and locks your message in a code, so only the right person can read it.

### Question 60

If you know the risks of sending a postcard but still ask for one, that can be your choice — after a warning.

### Question 61

Follow the office rulebook before sending private results, like checking the map before a long trip.

### Question 62

When you want to share something private, use the locked portal, not a megaphone.

### Question 63

In an emergency you call 911, just like you pull a fire alarm instead of writing a note.

### Question 64

Share private news through a locked channel, not by shouting it where everyone can hear.

### Question 65

A reminder should be like a short note — just enough to say when, nothing private.

### Question 66

Send only what is needed, in a sealed envelope — nothing extra, nothing public.

### Question 67

Before sending private results, check the office rules and make sure you are sending to the right person.

### Question 68

Use the safe, locked channel for private details — never a public post or an open text.

### Question 69

You check someone's ID before giving them a new key — otherwise anyone could claim to be the patient.

### Question 70

Lock the door when you leave so no one can walk into your account.

### Question 71

If private mail lands in the wrong tray, move it carefully to the right secure place — do not leave it lying around.

### Question 72

If someone keeps trying keys in your front door, you tell someone in charge.

### Question 73

If someone else is allowed to manage an account, set it up officially with permission — do not hand over a password.

### Question 74

When a health question needs an expert, pass the note to the expert instead of guessing.

### Question 75

Chest pain is like a smoke alarm — you do not wait or ignore it; you act fast.
